facts.statement: Harpagofututor was an extinct eel-like cartilaginous fish that lived during the Early Carboniferous period.
facts.quote: Harpagofututor is an extinct genus of eel-like cartilaginous fish from the Early Carboniferous (Mississippian).

facts.statement: Complete specimens of Harpagofututor were found in the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana, and an isolated tooth was found in Whitrope, Scotland.
facts.quote: It is primarily known from complete specimens discovered in the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana, as well as an isolated tooth from Whitrope, Scotland.

facts.statement: The genus Harpagofututor was first described in 1982 by the palaeontologist Richard Lund.
facts.quote: Harpagofututor was first described in 1982, from several complete specimens discovered in the Bear Gulch Limestone of Montana by Adelphi University palaeontologist Richard Lund.

facts.statement: Harpagofututor belongs to the family Chondrenchelyidae, a group of Holocephali closely related to modern chimaeras.
facts.quote: The genus is placed in the family Chondrenchelyidae, which are suggested to be members of Holocephali, with their closest living relatives being chimaeras.

facts.statement: Harpagofututor had an elongate eel-like body ranging from 8.6 to 17 cm in length, featuring a long upper medial fin without a spine.
facts.quote: Harpagofututor had a long, elongate eel-like body (with known specimens ranging in length from 8.6 to 17 cm) with a long upper medial fin running along the upper surface of the body without a fin spine.

facts.statement: Harpagofututor possessed triangular tooth plates in both the upper and lower jaws, similar to those of living chimaeras.
facts.quote: The mouth has pairs of tooth plates in the upper and lower jaws, comparable to those of living chimaeras, which were triangular in shape.

facts.statement: The cephalic claspers of Harpagofututor were considerably longer than the skull and are unique to this genus.
facts.quote: These structures, which are considerably longer than the skull itself, are apparently unique to Harpagofututor and not found in Chondrenchelys.

facts.statement: Researchers believe the cephalic claspers of Harpagofututor were used during mating.
facts.quote: They are thought to have been used during mating.

facts.statement: Harpagofututor likely used its tooth plates to crush prey.
facts.quote: The tooth plates of Harpagofututor are thought to have been used to crush prey.

facts.statement: Harpagofututor lived between 326.9 and 323.6 million years ago during the Serpukhovian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Serpukhovian to Serpukhovian (326.9 to 323.6 million years ago)
